title: The Road
author: Cormac McCarthy
blurb: Unspecified global disaster triggers the end of civilisation; a decade on, the dregs of humanity have descended into cannibalism. A man and his young son make for the coast across a dead America, knowing every moment might be their last. This tale of paternal love and endurance in a terrifyingly bleak post-apocalyptic world powerfully brought home our fragility in the face of climate breakdown.
firstSentence: “When he woke in the woods in the dark and the cold of the night he’d reach out to touch the child sleeping beside him.”

title: Catch-22
author: Joseph Heller
blurb: Heller set his blackly comic satire on the absurdity and futility of war among US bomber crews stationed on an Italian island in the early 1940s. In asking how a sane person can survive insanity, it gave the world a new name for impossible situations – though the original title, Catch-18, was changed to avoid confusion with a now-forgotten novel called Mila 18.
firstSentence: “It was love at first sight.”

title: Pedro Páramo
author: Juan Rulfo
blurb: Spoiler alert: without this short book from the Mexican author, we might not have had one of the more famous works on this list. Gabriel García Márquez read it in one sitting when it was published; the next day, he began One Hundred Years of Solitude. In this surreal, time-shifting story, a son goes in search of his father, the tyrant Pedro Páramo, in the rural town of Comala, which is now inhabited by ghosts. It was the only novel the enigmatic Rulfo published in his lifetime.
firstSentence: “I came to Comala because I was told that my father, a man called Pedro Páramo, was living there.”

title: The Return of the Native
author: Thomas Hardy
blurb: Missed encounters and misunderstandings plague the young couples in this lyrical tragedy set in a wild area of Hardy’s fictional Wessex where locals make their living from harvesting the spiny gorse. An adder plays an especially fateful role.
firstSentence: “A Saturday afternoon in November was approaching the time of twilight, and the vast tract of unenclosed wild known as Egdon Heath embrowned itself moment by moment.”

title: The Known World
author: Edward P Jones
blurb: Written by a debut American novelist who had struggled with poverty and homelessness, this historical epic set in the antebellum south, about a freed Black man who becomes an enslaver himself, won a Pulitzer for its powerful storytelling and complex moral vision.
firstSentence: “The evening his master died he worked again well after he ended the day for the other adults, his own wife among them, and sent them back with hunger and tiredness to their cabins.”

title: Invisible Cities
author: Italo Calvino
blurb: The 13th-century Venetian explorer Marco Polo spins gorgeous prose poems about 55 fictional cities for Chinese emperor Kublai Khan – but why does he never mention his home town? “Every time I describe a city I am saying something about Venice.” There’s a rigorous mathematical pattern behind these playful meditations on art, belonging, culture and imagination: Calvino described the novel as a polyhedron.
firstSentence: “Leaving there and proceeding for three days toward the east, you reach Diomira, a city with sixty silver domes, bronze statues of all the gods, streets paved with lead, a crystal theatre, a golden cock that crows each morning on a tower.”

title: Sentimental Education
author: Gustave Flaubert
blurb: The initial reception for Sentimental Education was damning: critics attacked its loose structure and perceived lack of plot; Henry James dismissed it as “elaborately and massively dreary”. It has since been recognised as one of Flaubert’s most innovative works, tracing a young man’s unfulfilled love and drifting ambitions in mid-19th century France, in a portrait of disillusionment and emotional inertia.
firstSentence: “On the 15th of September, 1840, about six o’clock in the morning, the Ville-de-Montereau was steering towards the quay of Saint-Bernard, blowing off its heavy smoke.”

title: Life and Fate
author: Vasily Grossman
blurb: Ukrainian Jewish journalist Grossman was a witness to the battle of Stalingrad and the Nazi extermination camps; written in 1959, his epic of life on the eastern front during the second world war, suppressed by the regime and smuggled to the west after his death, is widely seen as the Soviet War and Peace.
firstSentence: "There was a low mist. You could see the glare of headlamps reflected on the high-voltage cables beside the road.”

title: Jacob's Room
author: Virginia Woolf
blurb: Impressionistic and fragmentary, Jacob’s Room was the first of Woolf’s experimental novels. Piecing together the life of Jacob Flanders through conversations, memories and the perceptions of others, the novel traces his young life from childhood to Cambridge and on to London. Seen as an elegy for her brother Thoby, who died of typhoid aged 26, it raises questions about the futility of war and the impossibility of knowing another person. In her diaries, Woolf noted, “I think Jacob was a necessary step for me, in working free.”
firstSentence: "'So of course,' wrote Betty Flanders, pressing her heels rather deeper in the sand, 'there was nothing for it but to leave.'”

title: The Left Hand of Darkness
author: Ursula K Le Guin
blurb: A traveller to an icebound planet finds a society without gender: the inhabitants of Gethen are androgynous, only taking on either male or female sexual attributes when they enter a window of fertility. A groundbreaking feminist thought experiment from one of fantasy’s most interesting and humane voices.
firstSentence: “I’ll make my report as if I told a story, for I was taught as a child on my homeworld that Truth is a matter of the imagination.”

title: Ragtime
author: EL Doctorow
blurb: Set in the melting pot of jazz-era New York, with real figures – Henry Ford, JP Morgan, Harry Houdini – mingling with three fictional families, one Black, one Jewish, one white. This is a historical novel that brings the past roaring back to life; Barack Obama once called Doctorow his favourite author after Shakespeare.
firstSentence: “In 1902 Father built a house at the crest of the Broadview Avenue hill in New Rochelle, New York.”

title: The Line of Beauty
author: Alan Hollinghurst
blurb: After moving to London to do a PhD on Henry James, small-town boy Nick Guest is embraced – up to a point – by the glamorous Fedden family, and thrust into a world of fine art, cocaine and Tory politics. Hollinghurst paints a discomfiting portrait of an outsider in a world of privilege, and brilliantly conjures the excess and hypocrisy of England in the 80s – complete with a surprising cameo from Margaret Thatcher.
firstSentence: "Peter Crowther’s book on the election was already in the shops."

title: The Turn of the Screw
author: Henry James
blurb: When a governess is sent to an isolated country house to look after two orphans, she becomes convinced that evil spirits are haunting her charges. A classic ghost story, James’s claustrophobic tale was inspired by a story told to him by the Archbishop of Canterbury. James described it as a “shameless potboiler”, but his eerie and ambiguous novella has inspired many spin-offs, from Benjamin Britten’s 1954 opera to 1961 film The Innocents, on which Truman Capote worked as a screenwriter.
firstSentence: “The story had held us, round the fire, sufficiently breathless, but except the obvious remark that it was gruesome, as, on Christmas Eve in an old house, a strange tale should essentially be, I remember no comment uttered till somebody happened to say that it was the only case he had met in which such a visitation had fallen on a child.”

title: The Vegetarian
author: Han Kang
blurb: Deborah Smith’s translation introduced the Korean author to western audiences, winning the International Booker prize in 2016. The tripartite story centres on a woman who refuses to eat meat after a series of violent dreams, and is ultimately admitted to an asylum. Han would go on to win the Nobel prize in literature in 2024.
firstSentence: “Before my wife turned vegetarian, I’d always thought of her as completely unremarkable in every way.”

title: The Talented Mr Ripley
author: Patricia Highsmith
blurb: In her five novels about conman Tom Ripley, Highsmith created a character both morally repugnant and undeniably sympathetic. Ripley is a ruthless, sinister social climber, and yet it is impossible not to root for him in this tale of glamour and greed set on Italy’s Amalfi coast. A film-maker’s favourite, Ripley has been played by Matt Damon, John Malkovich and most recently by Andrew Scott.
firstSentence: “Tom glanced behind him and saw the man coming out of the Green Cage, heading his way.”

title: A Farewell to Arms
author: Ernest Hemingway
blurb: Partly based on Hemingway’s own experiences during the first world war, this is an American soldier’s memoir of his time serving as a medic with the Italian army, and a love affair with an English nurse that ends in tragedy. Hemingway wrote nearly 50 possible versions of the ending, and made a list of more than 30 possible titles; but after he sent a draft to F Scott Fitzgerald who returned it with pages of edits, he famously wrote back with the words “Kiss my ass”.
firstSentence: “In the late summer of that year we lived in a house in a village that looked across the river and the plain to the mountains.”

title: The End of the Affair
author: Graham Greene
blurb: The affair between novelist Maurice Bendrix and Sarah Miles (clearly based on the author’s long affair with his goddaughter) ends when Sarah makes a deal with God during the blitz. Betrayal, morality, faith – all Greene’s big themes are contained in this slim, intimate novel set around a rainy Clapham Common. Greene’s friend and fellow Catholic convert Evelyn Waugh said the story was “a singularly beautiful and moving one”.
firstSentence: “A story has no beginning or end; arbitrarily one chooses that moment of experience from which to look back or from which to look ahead.”

title: Buddenbrooks
author: Thomas Mann
blurb: Mann published this chronicle of the financial and spiritual decay of a wealthy 19th-century German family when he was in his mid-twenties, and caused a scandal for drawing on the society around him. William Faulkner saw it as the greatest novel of the 20th century, while “the Buddenbrooks effect” has come to refer to the tendency of family businesses to decline over the generations.
firstSentence: “And – and – what comes next?”

title: Rebecca
author: Daphne du Maurier
blurb: It has one of the most famous opening lines in literature and, in housekeeper Mrs Danvers, one of the most sinister female villains – plus an eponymous heroine who is dead from the off. The country estate in the novel was inspired by Du Maurier’s house in Cornwall. Critical opinion has always been a little snooty about this gothic triumph, but, like the glamorous Rebecca, its spell is impossible to shake off.
firstSentence: “Last night I dreamt I went to Manderley again.”

title: Go Tell It on the Mountain
author: James Baldwin
blurb: Baldwin’s first novel drew on his relationship with his cruel and controlling stepfather, an evangelical preacher from New Orleans. The story, set over a 24-hour period, centres on John Grimes, who is expected to follow the path of his abusive preacher father Gabriel. The novel, which connects sexuality with spirituality, has often been a target of book banning in the US.
firstSentence: "Everyone had always said that John would be a preacher when he grew up, just like his father."

title: A House for Mr Biswas
author: VS Naipaul
blurb: Naipaul’s international breakthrough came with his fourth novel, a comic epic set in postcolonial Trinidad following the doomed life of Mr Biswas, a character inspired by Naipaul’s father (the son in the novel, Anand, is based on the writer himself). Mr Biswas spends the novel living in a series of unsuitable homes – most of which are owned by his in-laws, with whom he’s constantly at war – until he finds the house of the title. Naipaul would go on to win the Nobel prize in literature in 2001.
firstSentence: “Ten weeks before he died, Mr. Mohun Biswas, a journalist of Sikkim Street, St. James, Port of Spain, was sacked.”

title: The Rainbow
author: DH Lawrence
blurb: For Lawrence’s characters, yearning has a transcendental quality and falling in love is a religious experience. This novel, set in rural Nottinghamshire and focused on three generations of a family amid the industrial change of the 19th century, was ruled obscene over a plotline concerning the lesbian relationship between the young Ursula Brangwen and her schoolteacher. Its sequel, Women in Love, was published in 1920.
firstSentence: “The Brangwens had lived for generations on the Marsh Farm, in the meadows where the Erewash twisted sluggishly through alder trees, separating Derbyshire from Nottinghamshire.”

title: My Ántonia
author: Willa Cather
blurb: Cather’s best known book is the story of immigrants to Nebraska and an indelible portrait of the midwest in the late 19th century. HL Mencken called the novel “one of the best that any American has done”. The hardships of life on the frontier, the resourcefulness of the people and the central place of migration in the American story are evoked in luminous prose.
firstSentence: “I first heard of Ántonia on what seemed to me an interminable journey across the great midland plain of North America.”

title: Dracula
author: Bram Stoker
blurb: Never out of print, this epistolary gothic horror – in which an English solicitor visits the castle of a Transylvanian nobleman who turns out to be a vampire, and who later lands by boat at Whitby on a mission to terrorise London – occupies a huge place in the culture. Stoker added details to existing folklore that have since become canon: that vampires must be invited over the threshold, and that they have no reflection in mirrors.
firstSentence: 3 May. Bistritz. – Left Munich at 8:35pm on 1st May, arriving at Vienna early next morning; should have arrived at 6:46, but the train was an hour late.”

title: The Bluest Eye
author: Toni Morrison
blurb: Eleven-year-old Pecola Breedlove dreams of having blue eyes like Shirley Temple. As she grows up in Lorain, Ohio (where Morrison was born) after the depression, life has taught Pecola that she is too small, too ugly and too Black. By putting a Black girl at the centre of her story, Morrison’s slim, devastating first novel changed American fiction. But it would be many years before her achievement was recognised. “The initial publication of The Bluest Eye was like Pecola’s life: dismissed, trivialised, misread,” she wrote in 1993.
firstSentence: “Quiet as it’s kept, there were no marigolds in the fall of 1941. We thought at the time it was because Pecola was having her father’s baby that the marigolds did not grow.”

title: Nervous Conditions
author: Tsitsi Dangarembga
blurb: The first novel published in English by a Black woman from Zimbabwe, Dangarembga’s semi-autobiographical debut tells the story of a rural girl’s dreams of education and escape. Now the first part of a trilogy, this instalment won the Commonwealth Writers’ prize and became a key text in postcolonial literature. The most recent, This Mournable Body, was shortlisted for the Booker in 2020. In the same year, she was arrested in Harare for her part in an anti-government demonstration. A conviction in 2022 was overturned a year later.
firstSentence: “I was not sorry when my brother died.”

title: Austerlitz
author: WG Sebald
blurb: The German writer’s melancholy, otherworldly books combine travel writing, biography, history and fiction, interposed with mysterious black and white photographs, to create a new genre and way of seeing – the Sebaldian. All are a response to the trauma of the Holocaust; this final book, about an architectural historian who escaped the Nazis on a Kindertransport, made him a contender for the Nobel, but he was to die the same year in a car crash at only 57.
firstSentence: “In the second half of the 1960s I traveled repeatedly from England to Belgium, partly for study purposes, partly for other reasons which were never entirely clear to me, staying sometimes for just one or two days, sometimes for several weeks.”

title: Our Mutual Friend
author: Charles Dickens
blurb: Money, hidden identities, the dust that London is built on: Dickens’s final completed novel continues his fascination with melodrama, class and mortality. While writing the serial, he had his own brush with death, rescuing the manuscript from a traumatic train crash. Contemporary readers thought the book overcomplicated, but 20th-century critics found it to prefigure modernist experimentation and the end of Victorian certainties.
firstSentence: “In these times of ours, though concerning the exact year there is no need to be precise, a boat of dirty and disreputable appearance, with two figures in it, floated on the Thames, between Southwark Bridge which is of iron, and London Bridge which is of stone, as an autumn evening was closing in.”

title: Kindred
author: Octavia E Butler
blurb: Described by the author as a “grim kind of fantasy”, Kindred is a landmark speculative novel that blends time travel with the brutal realities of American slavery. The story follows a modern Black woman repeatedly pulled back into the antebellum south, and explores the legacy of racist violence and the complexities of interracial relationships. A defining work of Afrofuturism, which fuses science fiction with racial justice, the novel has become one of Butler’s most influential and enduring works.
firstSentence: “I lost an arm on my last trip home.”

title: The Outsider
author: Albert Camus
blurb: In this classic existentialist novella, Meursault is a French settler in Algiers who remains chillingly detached from his environment and actions – whether that’s the death of his mother in an old people’s home or his own incarceration after he shoots an unnamed Arab man on the beach. In the UK, the title The Outsider was chosen on its translation in 1946, rather than the literal equivalent The Stranger (as it’s known in the US). The book’s portrait of colonialism, absurdism and “the benign indifference of the universe” has been endlessly influential, not least on English band the Cure’s first single in 1978, Killing an Arab.
firstSentence: “Maman died today.”

title: Jude the Obscure
author: Thomas Hardy
blurb: Dubbed “Jude the Obscene” on publication, Hardy’s final novel follows working-class stonemason Jude Fawley, who longs for an education. Hardy’s most overtly political novel, it explores controversial themes of class, religion, bigamy and a critique of marriage. The critical reception was so harsh, Hardy never wrote another novel, and turned instead to poetry, but it has since been celebrated as a powerful and radical critique of Victorian society.
firstSentence: “The schoolmaster was leaving the village, and everybody seemed sorry.”

title: Crime and Punishment
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
blurb: In a novel that brilliantly exposes the gulf between sterile theorising and real human relations, impoverished former student Raskolnikov decides to commit a murder to prove a point – that some people are of no consequence, while others are so extraordinary that moral laws don’t apply to them. Unfortunately, his conscience doesn’t cooperate. Racked by guilt, haunted by bad dreams and encouraged by the woman he comes to love, he is driven to confess.
firstSentence: “On an exceptionally hot evening early in July a young man came out of the garret in which he lodged in S. Place and walked slowly, as though in hesitation, towards K. bridge.”

title: Blood Meridian
author: Cormac McCarthy
blurb: This brutal anti-western, McCarthy’s fifth novel, is partly the coming-of-age story of 14-year-old Tennessean “the kid”, who winds up joining a band of violent outlaws. Here, McCarthy fictionalises the atrocities of the Glanton gang, a group of white “scalp hunters” who terrorised Indigenous people on the US-Mexico border in the mid-19th century. Praised for its lyricism, the novel is widely considered McCarthy’s magnum opus.
firstSentence: “See the child.”

title: The Man Without Qualities
author: Robert Musil
blurb: More than 20 years in the writing, exceeding 1,000 pages in three unfinished volumes, this modernist masterpiece from an author widely seen as the Austrian Proust is set in 1913 Vienna, in the dying days of the Austro-Hungarian empire. The protagonist is a mathematician in the grip of existential crisis, reflecting on the meaning and meaninglessness of the world around him. “No novelist is dearer to me,” said Milan Kundera.
firstSentence: “There was a depression over the Atlantic.”

title: The Master and Margarita
author: Mikhail Bulgakov
blurb: In this satire of the Soviet Union, written between 1928 and 1940, the devil and his entourage – including a vampire and an enormous black cat – cause mayhem in officially atheistic Moscow. Like his character the Master, who is writing a novel about Pontius Pilate, and fearing censorship and persecution by the authorities, Bulgakov burned the first manuscript in 1930; the darkly playful fable of good and evil went on to inspire the Rolling Stones’s Sympathy for the Devil.
firstSentence: “At the sunset hour of one warm spring day two men were to be seen at Patriarch’s Ponds.”

title: The Color Purple
author: Alice Walker
blurb: An extraordinary late flowering of the epistolary novel, it tells a powerfully moving story of abuse, love and female solidarity through letters sent by its heroine, Celie, initially to God, and then to her sister, Nettie. Across 30 years in the Jim Crow south, she records the worst and the best of humanity. The 1985 film adaptation, directed by Steven Spielberg, starred Whoopi Goldberg and Oprah Winfrey.
firstSentence: “You better not never tell nobody but God. It’d kill your mammy.”

title: The Good Soldier
author: Ford Madox Ford
blurb: Ford hated the title of his torrid tale of adultery, chaos and suicide among two couples: a novel dripping in irony, with a narrator who is not to be trusted. He’d wanted to call it The Saddest Story, a title thought too downbeat by his publishers during a time of war. Ford’s messy personal life chimes with his fiction: an affair with Jean Rhys inspired novels by him, her and Rhys’s husband.
firstSentence: “This is the saddest story I have ever heard.”

title: White Teeth
author: Zadie Smith
blurb: This smart, funny, big-hearted novel bounces around multicultural north-west London, where Smith grew up. A sprawling, multigenerational saga, its cast includes British Army vet Archie Jones and his best friend Samad Iqbal, an Islamist terrorist group with the acronym “Kevin”, a Jewish scientist genetically engineering a FutureMouse and Jehovah’s Witnesses who think that the world is about to end. Published to rapturous reviews when she was just 24 years old, this dazzling debut went on to sell 2m copies and launch a literary star.
firstSentence: “Early in the morning, late in the century, Cricklewood Broadway.”

title: Half of a Yellow Sun
author: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
blurb: Set in the 1960s during the Biafran war, Adichie’s second novel won the Women’s prize for fiction and became a bestseller. Inspired by her father’s memories of the war, in which both her grandfathers died, the novel follows the fortunes of houseboy Ugwu, and is a searing account of violence, politics, love and betrayal.
firstSentence: “Master was a little crazy; he had spent too many years reading books overseas, talked to himself in his office, did not always return greetings, and had too much hair.”

title: The Rings of Saturn
author: WG Sebald
blurb: A nameless narrator walks the Suffolk coast, musing on the weight of the past: from Chinese empresses to English imperialism, silkworms to the herring industry, Rembrandt to bombing campaigns. After Sebald’s death, a memorial bench in the shape of Saturn’s rings was built around a copper beech tree at the University of East Anglia, where he was a professor.
firstSentence: “In August 1992, when the dog days were drawing to an end, I set off to walk the county of Suffolk, in the hope of dispelling the emptiness that takes hold of me whenever I have completed a long stint of work.”

title: Howards End
author: EM Forster
blurb: Often glossed as a tale of two families and two contrasting approaches to life – the spirited and idealistic, the worldly and compromised – this is also a story about money: despite their apparent differences, the Schlegels and the Wilcoxes both “stand upon money as upon islands. It is so firm beneath our feet that we forget its very existence.” The fact that this isn’t the case for everyone intrudes dramatically into the plot. The Guardian’s February 1910 review described it as a book of “immense liberality”.
firstSentence: “One may as well begin with Helen’s letters to her sister.”

title: Never Let Me Go
author: Kazuo Ishiguro
blurb: Deceptively simple yet devastating. In Ishiguro’s sixth novel 31-year-old Kathy looks back at her childhood at Hailsham, a boarding school that we soon discover harbours a dark secret – why and for what purpose Kathy and her friends were created. Twenty years on, it remains Ishiguro’s most read novel. As he noted in a recent Guardian interview, “I’ve been praised for producing stuff that makes people cry. They gave me a Nobel prize for it.”
firstSentence: "My name is Kathy H.”

title: Disgrace
author: JM Coetzee
blurb: Coetzee’s South African masterpiece is a dark, destabilising account of sexual violence and the aftermath of apartheid. It made him the first author to win the Booker prize twice (his first win was for Life & Times of Michael K in 1983), though he declined to attend the ceremonies. In 2002, he emigrated to Australia, and the following year was awarded the Nobel prize in literature.
firstSentence: “For a man of his age, fifty-two, divorced, he has, to his mind, solved the problem of sex rather well.”

title: The Sound and the Fury
author: William Faulkner
blurb: The tale of a troubled family in the decaying American south, with daughter Caddy’s tragedy seen from the perspectives of her three brothers and a Black servant. Opening with the stream-of-consciousness thoughts of Benjy, who has severe intellectual disabilities, it’s notoriously challenging; though it was instrumental in winning Faulkner a Nobel, he admitted it was also “a real son-of-a-bitch”. His advice for those still struggling with his work after reading it two or three times? “Read it four times.”
firstSentence: “Through the fence, between the curling flower spaces, I could see them hitting.”

title: Mansfield Park
author: Jane Austen
blurb: Austen’s third novel follows impoverished Fanny Price, sent to live with her wealthy aunt and uncle Bertram at their grand estate. A follow-up to Pride and Prejudice, the novel sold out within six months, though with themes of loneliness, religion, class and colonialism, it proved less critically popular than its predecessors. It was later re-evaluated by postcolonial and feminist academics, most notably in Edward Said’s Jane Austen and Empire (1993).
firstSentence: “About thirty years ago Miss Maria Ward, of Huntingdon, with only seven thousand pounds, had the good luck to captivate Sir Thomas Bertram, of Mansfield Park, in the county of Northampton …”

title: The Waves
author: Virginia Woolf
blurb: This poetic, experimental novel follows six friends from nursery to old age through interconnected interior monologues. In 1929, as she began her modernist masterpiece, Woolf wrote in her diary: “I think I am about to embody at last the exact shapes my brain holds.”
firstSentence: “The sun had not yet risen.”

title: Orlando
author: Virginia Woolf
blurb: Woolf’s lover and muse Vita Sackville-West inspired this fabulous fictional biography of Orlando, who begins the book as a young nobleman in Elizabethan England, travels to Constantinople, and later transforms into a woman. Spanning 300 years, it is a satire on gender roles and, as Sackville-West’s son Nigel Nicolson famously described it, “the longest and most charming love letter in literature”. Tilda Swinton starred as the immortal poet in Sally Potter’s acclaimed 1992 film adaptation.
firstSentence: “He – for there could be no doubt of his sex, though the fashion of the time did something to disguise it – was in the act of slicing at the head of a Moor which swung from the rafters.”

title: The Transit of Venus
author: Shirley Hazzard
blurb: Two orphan sisters, Caroline and Grace Bell, leave Australia for postwar England, attempting to build new lives amid shifting social landscapes. Often compared to Henry James for its psychological precision, Hazzard rejected the influence in a 2006 Guardian interview, saying: “There is a myth that I was raised on James. I had hardly read anything of him when I started to write.” She added: “I think I’m funnier than Henry James.”
firstSentence: "By nightfall the headlines would be reporting devastation."

title: The Golden Bowl
author: Henry James
blurb: Henry James’s final completed novel is a study of marriage, adultery and the meeting of English and American cultures. It focuses almost exclusively on the consciousness and interiority of the central characters – as a result, contemporary readers and critics often found the novel impenetrable. Now, however, it is regarded as one of the key works of James’s “late phase”, alongside The Wings of the Dove and The Ambassadors.
firstSentence: “The Prince had always liked his London, when it had come to him; he was one of the modern Romans who find by the Thames a more convincing image of the truth of the ancient state than any they have left by the Tiber.”

title: My Brilliant Friend
author: Elena Ferrante
blurb: The first in Ferrante’s Neapolitan Quartet, My Brilliant Friend follows Lila and Lenù, two girls growing up in a poor neighbourhood in 1950s Naples. The intensity and rivalry of their friendship is set against a backdrop of social and political upheaval as the girls struggle to escape their suffocating community. Translated by Ann Goldstein, the novel became a global phenomenon, leading to fierce speculation about the pseudonymous author’s true identity.
firstSentence: “This morning Rino telephoned.”

title: Wide Sargasso Sea
author: Jean Rhys
blurb: This postcolonial prequel to Jane Eyre takes up the story of the first Mrs Rochester. Swapping Charlotte Brontë’s cold, dark gothic for the oppressive sunshine of the Caribbean, Dominica-born Rhys reimagines Brontë’s notorious “madwoman in the attic” as a Creole heiress called Antoinette Cosway. After decades of obscurity, its critical success propelled Rhys back into the spotlight at the age of 76, with Angela Carter hailing the novel as “a complete reimagining of what literature can do”.
firstSentence: “They say when trouble comes close ranks, and so the white people did.”

title: A Fine Balance
author: Rohinton Mistry
blurb: Mistry originally conceived of A Fine Balance as a short novel. Starting simply with the image of a woman at a sewing machine, it subsequently grew into a 700-page epic, as Mistry became increasingly absorbed in the backstories of the tailors and the student who come to share the seamstress's life. Set in an unidentified city in India, initially during the emergency in 1975 and later in 1984, it follows four strangers from distinct backgrounds whose lives are brought together as they navigate political repression and poverty.
firstSentence: “The morning express bloated with passengers slowed to a crawl, then lurched forward suddenly, as though to resume full speed.”

title: The Metamorphosis
author: Franz Kafka
blurb: Kafka took just three weeks to write his absurdist novella about Gregor Samsa, the travelling salesman who wakes to find himself transformed into a bug. The story has been endlessly referenced and reimagined, from the cover of the Rolling Stones’s 1975 compilation album featuring the band members as bugs, to Ian McEwan’s 2019 novella The Cockroach, in which an insect takes over the body of the UK prime minister.
firstSentence: “As Gregor Samsa awoke one morning from uneasy dreams he found himself transformed in his bed into a gigantic insect.”

title: Vanity Fair
author: William Makepeace Thackeray
blurb: Early versions of Vanity Fair carried the subtitle A Novel Without a Hero, reflecting Thackeray’s rejection of Victorian fiction’s saintly heroines and cartoonish villains. Set during the Napoleonic era, it is a satire of social ambition, its characters shifting between virtue and vanity. Its legacy endures, perhaps most famously living on in the title of the lifestyle magazine.
firstSentence: “While the present century was in its teens, and on one sunshiny morning in June, there drove up to the great iron gate of Miss Pinkerton’s academy for young ladies, on Chiswick Mall, a large family coach, with two fat horses in blazing harness, driven by a fat coachman in a three-cornered hat and wig, at the rate of four miles an hour.”

title: The Leopard
author: Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa
blurb: An old order crumbles in this exquisitely styled, gem-like novel as the head of an aristocratic family witnesses its power and prestige gradually dissolve in the political upheaval of Italian unification. The passing of time and the ephemeral nature of power are the themes of Lampedusa’s only novel, which came out posthumously after being rejected by publishers in his lifetime. Lampedusa was the last in a line of princes; the Italian title Il Gattopardo actually refers to a different big cat, the serval, which appears in the Lampedusa coat of arms.
firstSentence: “The daily recital of the Rosary was over.”

title: The Golden Notebook
author: Doris Lessing
blurb: Blending political critique with psychological realism and an experimental form, The Golden Notebook explores communism, anti-Stalinism, the sexual revolution and the contradictions of women’s liberation. Lessing, an outspoken critic of apartheid who was banned from South Africa and Rhodesia in 1956, was deeply engaged in the political currents of her time. Reflecting on the novel’s feminist legacy, she said in a 1994 interview: “Things have changed for white, middle-class women, but nothing has changed outside this group.”
firstSentence: “The two women were alone in the London flat.”

title: Giovanni's Room
author: James Baldwin
blurb: Before the release of Giovanni’s Room, Baldwin had been acclaimed for Go Tell It on the Mountain (on our list at 79), a novel rooted in his adolescence in 1930s Harlem that led many to position him as a writer of “Black fiction”. It was a label he resisted, and for his next novel, he chose to explore homosexuality and masculinity through the perspective of white characters. The book was highly controversial for its candid depiction of sexuality, desire and internalised homophobia, and rejected several times before its publication.
firstSentence: “I stand at the window of this great house in the south of France as night falls, the night which is leading me to the most terrible morning of my life.”

title: Housekeeping
author: Marilynne Robinson
blurb: What is home? What is family? What makes for a good life? Robinson’s mysterious, dreamlike novel probes profound questions in richly metaphorical prose. A study of loss and loneliness, it centres on orphaned sisters Ruthie and Lucille Stone, who live in a lakeside house in the fictional town of Fingerbone in remote north-west America, under the care of their eccentric guardian Aunt Sylvie. Robinson has said that Fingerbone was based on the town where she grew up, and that the vastness of that landscape “had a huge religious implication for me”.
firstSentence: “My name is Ruth.”

title: The Magic Mountain
author: Thomas Mann
blurb: Mann’s epic tale of European civilisation on the brink of war takes place in an unlikely setting: an otherworldly tuberculosis sanatorium high in the Swiss Alps. After making the questionable decision to visit his cousin, who is undergoing a course of treatment there, Hans Castorp finds himself unable to leave – and beguiled by the philosophical, political and romantic currents that seem to converge there. The sanatorium Mann based his story around is now a hotel that hosts attendees of the World Economic Forum in nearby Davos.
firstSentence: “An unassuming young man was travelling, in midsummer, from his native city of Hamburg to Davos-Platz in the Canton of the Grisons, on a three weeks’ visit.”

title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad
blurb: Conrad drew on his 1890 journey to Congo Free State, a private colony under vicious subjugation by the Belgian king, for the story of a sea captain’s mission to find a European ivory trader who has gone rogue. The novella revealed the monstrosity at the heart of the imperial project, but has drawn its own accusations of racism – not least from Chinua Achebe, whose riposte Things Fall Apart appears at No 22 on our list. The 1979 film Apocalypse Now, starring Marlon Brando as Colonel Kurtz, brilliantly transposes the horror to Vietnam and Cambodia.
firstSentence: “The Nellie, a cruising yawl, swung to her anchor without a flutter of the sails, and was at rest.”

title: Song of Solomon
author: Toni Morrison
blurb: Following the life of Macon “Milkman” Dead III as he grows up in mid-century Michigan and later travels through the South in search of family history and a sense of belonging, Song of Solomon was Morrison’s breakout novel. She wrote much of it while working full-time as an editor at Random House, often drafting it in the early mornings before her children woke.
firstSentence: “The North Carolina Mutual Life Insurance agent promised to fly from Mercy to the other side of Lake Superior at three o’clock.”

title: Their Eyes Were Watching God
author: Zora Neale Hurston
blurb: Hurston’s second novel, written in seven weeks, was published at the twilight of the Harlem Renaissance, and is now considered a classic of the movement, particularly for its incorporation of folklore and southern African American dialect. The novel follows the life and romantic trials of Janie, who has two doomed marriages before meeting her real love, Tea Cake, who lets her be free.
firstSentence: “Ships at a distance have every man’s wish on board.”

title: The Age of Innocence
author: Edith Wharton
blurb: Set in 1870s upper-class, gilded age New York, Wharton’s eighth novel is a closely observed portrait of manners, desire and social constraint. It won the 1921 Pulitzer prize for fiction, making Wharton the first woman to receive the award. (The jury had originally chosen Sinclair Lewis’s Main Street, but the trustees rejected it as unwholesome.) It has been adapted for screen numerous times, most famously in Martin Scorsese’s 1993 film, starring Daniel Day-Lewis, Michelle Pfeiffer and Winona Ryder.
firstSentence: “On a January evening of the early seventies, Christine Nilsson was singing in Faust at the Academy of Music in New York.”

title: Invisible Man
author: Ralph Ellison
blurb: The only one of Ellison’s novels published during his lifetime, Invisible Man is a landmark exploration of race and identity in 20th-century America. Ellison spent seven years writing the novel, which follows an unnamed Black narrator confronting racism and his own sense of self. It won the 1953 US National book award, making Ellison the first African American writer to receive the prize, and has had a lasting influence, cited by Barack Obama as a major inspiration for his memoir Dreams from My Father.
firstSentence: “I am an invisible man.”

title: The Handmaid's Tale
author: Margaret Atwood
blurb: “One of my rules was that I would not put any events into the book that had not already happened.” Atwood’s dystopia draws on real-world oppression, from early American puritans to the Islamic revolution in Iran, to create a chillingly plausible fundamentalist America in which women are forbidden to read and write, with “handmaids” used as brood mares for the elite.
firstSentence: “We slept in what had once been the gymnasium.”

title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens
blurb: From the opening graveyard scene where orphan Pip first encounters the convict Magwitch, Dickens’s coming-of-age novel grips the imagination and doesn’t let go. A story of social mobility and moral corruption, its cast of unforgettable characters includes jilted spinster Miss Havisham, who haunts her mansion in tattered veil and gown, training her young charge Estella to take revenge on men. On the advice of friends, Dickens reluctantly changed his original ending to one that allowed for the possibility that Pip and Estella end up together.
firstSentence: “My father’s family name being Pirrip, and my Christian name Philip, my infant tongue could make of both names nothing longer or more explicit than Pip.”

title: Wolf Hall
author: Hilary Mantel
blurb: The first instalment of Mantel’s epic three-part account of Thomas Cromwell’s ascent at the court of Henry VIII won her the Booker prize – the follow-up, Bring Up the Bodies, made her the first woman and first British writer to win the prize twice. The first line of Wolf Hall came to Mantel upon waking up one morning.
firstSentence: “'So now get up.'”

title: David Copperfield
author: Charles Dickens
blurb: Dickens wrote: “of all my books I like this best”. Partly autobiographical, it follows the eponymous hero from impoverished childhood to adult success as a respected author. Stuffed with memorable characters, from his eccentric great aunt Betsey Trotwood to the “ever so humble” Uriah Heep, it was a critical and commercial smash. Barbara Kingsolver’s 2022 reimagining, Demon Copperhead, transposed the action from early Victorian England to opioid-ravaged Appalachia to explore similar themes of injustice and social mobility.
firstSentence: “Whether I shall turn out to be the hero of my own life, or whether that station will be held by anybody else, these pages must show.”

title: The God of Small Things
author: Arundhati Roy
blurb: Following seven-year-old twins Rahel and Estha as they move with their mother to their grandparents’ home in the Kerala village of Ayemenem, Roy’s debut novel won the Booker prize and was an instant bestseller. The novel faced criticism and a legal case in India for alleged obscenity and criticism of the caste system. Roy remains a vocal critic of the Indian government, but didn’t write another novel for 20 years.
firstSentence: “May in Ayemenem is a hot, brooding month.”

title: The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie
author: Muriel Spark
blurb: “Give me a girl at an impressionable age and she is mine for life,” announces Spark’s charismatic teacher in this elegantly sinister study of favouritism, fascism and the power of persuasive fictions. Spark draws the reader into Miss Brodie’s cultured and elite clique – the “crème de la crème” – only to reveal that her romantic lessons on life and love hide a darker desire to control and manipulate.
firstSentence: “The boys, as they talked to the girls from Marcia Blaine School, stood on the far side of their bicycles holding the handlebars, which established a protective fence of bicycle between the sexes, and the impression that at any moment the boys were likely to be away.”

title: Frankenstein
author: Mary Shelley
blurb: Shelley was just 18 when she began work on Frankenstein, as part of a ghost story competition suggested by Byron during a rainy holiday on the banks of Lake Geneva. The tale of a scientist discovering the spark of life to create an 8ft-tall humanoid – sensitive, self-educated, vegetarian, but furiously vengeful after rejection by his progenitor – has become an essential part of the culture.
firstSentence: “I am by birth a Genevese, and my family is one of the most distinguished of that republic.”

title: Pale Fire
author: Vladimir Nabokov
blurb: A metafictional delight presenting a 999-line poem by a poet called John Shade, which is subverted by the commentary appended by his neighbour and colleague. Critics have argued endlessly over how to read this slyly witty meditation on meaning and madness; Nabokov described it as “full of plums that I keep hoping somebody will find” – including a minor character called Pnin and a hurricane by the name of Lolita.
firstSentence: “I was the shadow of the waxwing slain / By the false azure in the windowpane; I was the smudge of ashen fluff - and I / Lived on, flew on, in the reflected sky.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
blurb: Dostoevsky’s final novel, in which the murder of a cruel landowner throws suspicion on to his sons, tackles the biggest questions: good, evil, free will, original sin and the possibility of human redemption, all explored against the backdrop of a Russia in the grip of seismic social change. Both Einstein and Freud thought it the best novel ever written.
firstSentence: “Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov was the third son of Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, a land owner well known in our district in his own day, and still remembered among us owing to his gloomy and tragic death, which happened thirteen years ago, and which I shall describe in its proper place.”

title: The Trial
author: Franz Kafka
blurb: Kafka’s literary executor defied his request to burn all unpublished manuscripts after his death, and this unfinished fable of bureaucratic oppression, in which Josef K is inexplicably victimised by a shadowy authority, was published posthumously. Written during the first world war, it seems to prefigure both the totalitarianism and existential dread of the decades to come.
firstSentence: “Someone must have been telling lies about Josef K., for without having done anything wrong he was arrested one fine morning.”

title: Don Quixote
author: Miguel de Cervantes
blurb: This exuberant satire of chivalric romance – in which a middle-aged Spanish man who reads too many books decides to become a knight, enlisting a farmhand as his squire – is a sprawling comic portrait of obsession, friendship and the gulf between imagination and reality. It’s often seen as the first modern novel; part two, published a decade after the first in response to an impostor’s follow-up, included characters who had read part one – metafiction in the 17th century. The Don has given his name to an adjective for impractical, impulsive idealism.
firstSentence: “In a certain village in La Mancha, of which I cannot remember the name, there lived not long ago one of those old-fashioned gentlemen, who are never without a lance upon a rack, an old target, a lean horse, and a greyhound.”

title: Lolita
author: Vladimir Nabokov
blurb: The confession of paedophile Humbert Humbert, literature’s most dazzlingly unreliable narrator, is an endlessly controversial high-wire act. Published in France by Olympia Press, an imprint better known for releasing pornographic pulp, the first print run was just 5,000 copies. Branded obscene, the novel was swiftly banned there, and around the world, censors keeping copies out of the UK until 1959 and Australia until 1965. Writing in the Spectator, Kingsley Amis called it “bad as a work of art, and morally bad”. In his introduction to the 1992 Everyman edition his son Martin Amis hailed its brilliance, writing: “In common with its narrator, it is both irresistible and unforgivable.” It has now sold more than 50m copies.
firstSentence: “Lolita, light of my life, fire of my loins.”

title: The Remains of the Day
author: Kazuo Ishiguro
blurb: The Nobel laureate’s Booker winner is narrated by the emotionally repressed Stevens, a butler taking his first holiday from Darlington Hall, the grand stately home where he has worked for more than 30 years. As he looks back from 1956, it becomes clear that he has wasted his life in devotion to professional duty, loyalty to his Nazi-sympathising master thwarting any chance of personal happiness. A 1993 Merchant Ivory screen adaptation of the book starred Anthony Hopkins and Emma Thompson.
firstSentence: “It seems increasingly likely that I really will undertake the expedition that has been preoccupying my imagination now for some days.”

title: Midnight's Children
author: Salman Rushdie
blurb: In the hour after midnight on 15 August 1947, the beginning of India’s independence from British colonial rule and its partition from Pakistan, 1,001 children are born with supernatural powers. This exuberant magic realist epic, a dazzling allegory of the ensuing decades, won both the Booker of Bookers in 1993 and the Best of the Booker in 2008.
firstSentence: “I was born in the city of Bombay … once upon a time.”

title: Things Fall Apart
author: Chinua Achebe
blurb: A cornerstone of African literature, Achebe’s debut novel reshaped world literature. Set in 1890s Nigeria, it recounts the life of Okonkwo, a proud Igbo warrior, as colonial governors and Christian missionaries arrive in his village, disrupting the traditional tribal way of life. Looking back on his 18-year imprisonment on Robben Island, Nelson Mandela described how when he read it, “the prison walls fell down”.
firstSentence: “Okonkwo was well known throughout the nine villages and even beyond.”

title: The Portrait of a Lady
author: Henry James
blurb: Like many 19th-century novels, this first appeared in serial form before being released as a full book, with readers having to wait patiently to follow the fortunes of James’s protagonist Isabel Archer, a young American woman whose inheritance leads her into a troubled marriage. James wasn’t fully satisfied with the original version – he rewrote large portions for the 1908 “New York Edition”.
firstSentence: “Under certain circumstances there are few hours in life more agreeable than the hour dedicated to the ceremony known as afternoon tea.”

title: Wuthering Heights
author: Emily Brontë
blurb: Emerald Fennell’s maximalist, sexed-up film divided opinions on its release in February. The source text – Brontë’s only novel – was published under the pen name Ellis Bell, and was similarly polarising among its Victorian audience for its depiction of the destructive relationship of its antiheroes, Heathcliff and Cathy, and its moral ambivalence. Set on the blustery Yorkshire moors, it is considered a classic of gothic literature.
firstSentence: “1801. – I have just returned from a visit to my landlord – the solitary neighbour that I shall be troubled with.”

title: The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman
author: Laurence Sterne
blurb: Released in nine volumes, Sterne’s anarchic, experimental anti-novel is a metafictional autobiography in which the lead character isn’t born until several volumes in. This stunningly modern shaggy dog story is full of silly puns and philosophical digressions into everything from noses to nominative determinism and siege warfare. Its huge success transformed Sterne from an obscure Yorkshire clergyman into a literary celebrity.
firstSentence: “I wish either my father or my mother, or indeed both of them, as they were in duty both equally bound to it, had minded what they were about when they begot me ...”

title: Persuasion
author: Jane Austen
blurb: The final novel completed before Austen’s death, and seen as the most mature of her works, Persuasion is a quietly devastating account of missed opportunities and repressed love. Anne Elliot, persuaded to break off her engagement to Captain Wentworth, is confronted by what might have been when he comes into her life again seven years on. Though not as immediately popular as other Austen novels, it has won devoted fans in the years since.
firstSentence: “Sir Walter Elliot, of Kellynch Hall, in Somersetshire, was a man who, for his own amusement, never took up any book but the Baronetage …”

title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
author: Gabriel García Márquez
blurb: Colonialism and civil war, clouds of yellow butterflies, levitating priests and a plague of insomnia … Inspired by his childhood home in Aracataca, Colombia, and his grandparents’ stories, García Márquez’s magical realist masterpiece was written over an intense 18-month period, the novelist chain-smoking 60 cigarettes a day as he set down the funny, tragic, political history of a fictional Caribbean town called Macondo. Following the Buendía family over seven generations, this landmark of Latin American literature would go on to sell more than 50m copies around the world. García Márquez was awarded the Nobel prize in literature in 1982.
firstSentence: “Many years later, as he faced the firing squad, Colonel Aureliano Buendía was to remember that distant afternoon when his father took him to discover ice.”

title: Nineteen Eighty-Four
author: George Orwell
blurb: Arguably no novel has as much relevance to contemporary global politics as the final complete book by the author of Animal Farm, with “Orwellian” now regularly applied to governments seen to be taking a leaf from the playbook of Big Brother and the Party, the rulers of the dystopian autocratic state depicted in the novel. Orwell wrote the book while seriously ill with tuberculosis, from which he died in 1950.
firstSentence: “It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen.”

title: Moby-Dick
author: Herman Melville
blurb: The great American epic of obsession, set aboard the whaling ship Pequod, in which Captain Ahab is determined to hunt down the eponymous cetacean that bit off his leg (and left him with a whale jawbone as a prosthesis). Rich in symbolism, intellectual digression, cosmic complexity and bloodcurdling action alike, its greatness was appreciated only after Melville’s death; 80 years later, first mate Starbuck gave his name to a coffee chain.
firstSentence: “Call me Ishmael.”

title: Mrs Dalloway
author: Virginia Woolf
blurb: Past loves and paths not taken intrude on Clarissa Dalloway’s meticulous preparations for a society party in this dazzling stream-of-consciousness novel, set on an ordinary June day in 1920s London. Woolf’s ahead-of-their-time themes include same-sex desire (Sally, a youthful crush of Clarissa’s, turns up at the party as a married mother of five) and PTSD (Septimus, a veteran of the first world war, spirals towards madness).
firstSentence: “Mrs Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.”

title: Emma
author: Jane Austen
blurb: In Emma, the novelist famously set out to create “a heroine whom no one but myself will much like”. As her privileged, overconfident protagonist meddles and matchmakes her way towards self-knowledge, Austen’s perfectly plotted tale interrogates wealth, class and social power through the study of her ideal subject: “three or four families in a country village”. The last novel published in Austen’s lifetime, it was adapted into 1995 Hollywood high-school comedy Clueless, starring Alicia Silverstone and Paul Rudd.
firstSentence: “Emma Woodhouse, handsome, clever, and rich, with a comfortable home and happy disposition, seemed to unite some of the best blessings of existence; and had lived nearly twenty-one years in the world with very little to distress or vex her.”

title: Bleak House
author: Charles Dickens
blurb: The saga of Jarndyce and Jarndyce, a legal case over conflicting wills that swallows all it encounters, is a towering portrait of foggy, fantastical London. Widely seen as Dickens’s finest achievement, it features one of literature’s most controversial deaths (Mr Krook, by spontaneous combustion).
firstSentence: “London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting in Lincoln’s Inn Hall.”

title: The Great Gatsby
author: F Scott Fitzgerald
blurb: This lushly written tragedy of corruption among the “careless people” revelling in jazz-age hedonism didn’t become a hit until the second world war, when free copies were distributed to US soldiers. It captures the hollowness at the heart of the American dream, through an outsider’s view of the elite.
firstSentence: “In my younger and more vulnerable years my father gave me some advice that I’ve been turning over in my mind ever since.”

title: Madame Bovary
author: Gustave Flaubert
blurb: A devastating cautionary tale about the dangers of fantasy, snobbery and romantic yearning, the story of frustrated doctor’s wife Emma Bovary transformed the novel with its meticulous rendering of small-town life in mid-19th-century France. Scholars note that there is no record of Flaubert ever saying “Madame Bovary, c’est moi”, the quote often attributed to him as evidence for the ultimately autobiographical nature of all fiction.
firstSentence: “We were in class when the head-master came in, followed by a ‘new fellow,’ not wearing the school uniform, and a school servant carrying a large desk.”

title: Pride and Prejudice
author: Jane Austen
blurb: Austen’s second published novel gave us Lizzy Bennet, Mr Darcy – and arguably the original romantic comedy. The ironic humour, the lovable Bennet clan and the brooding, arrogant Darcy have inspired ardent fans ever since, with popular adaptations ranging from the classic 90s TV drama to the Keira Knightley film, and of course the inspiration for Mark Darcy in Helen Fielding’s Bridget Jones series.
firstSentence: “It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.”

title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Brontë
blurb: The tale of poor governess Jane, her unlikely love affair with Mr Rochester, and the madwoman in his attic was a bestseller on publication. (Her sister Emily’s novel Wuthering Heights came out two months later.) Published under the pen name Currer Bell, its innovative first-person narrative, gothic and erotic themes thrilled contemporary readers.
firstSentence: “There was no possibility of taking a walk that day.”

title: War and Peace
author: Leo Tolstoy
blurb: Combining love, tragedy, philosophy and a history of the Napoleonic wars, Tolstoy claimed his four-volume epic was “not a novel”; Dostoevsky disagreed, describing it as the masterpiece of Russian literature. Though the first part of the work was serialised in the Russian Messenger in 1865, earlier versions are thought to date back to 1856, and Tolstoy is said to have redrafted it as many as 20 times.
firstSentence: “Well, Prince, so Genoa and Lucca are now just family estates of the Buonapartes.”

title: Anna Karenina
author: Leo Tolstoy
blurb: The tale of a doomed love affair between Anna, wife of Karenin, and Count Vronsky, Tolstoy’s first “true novel”, as he saw it, was serialised over two years before being published to a mixed reception. While Tolstoy himself found the novel to be “beastly”, readers ever since have been drawn in by the depth of emotion and the breadth of his depiction of Russian society; William Faulkner declared it the greatest novel ever written.
firstSentence: “Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.”

title: In Search of Lost Time
author: Marcel Proust
blurb: First translated into English in 1922, Proust’s seven-volume Parisian epic holds the world record for longest novel. Used today to describe how a sensory experience can trigger involuntary memories, the term “madeleine effect” (or “Proustian rush”) originates from a scene in the first few pages where the world-weary narrator dips a small cake in lime-blossom tea and is transported back to his childhood.
firstSentence: “For a long time I used to go to bed early.”

title: To the Lighthouse
author: Virginia Woolf
blurb: Woolf’s fifth novel is set mainly across two days, 10 years apart – either side of the first world war – and slips between the perspectives of the Ramsay family and their guests at their summer house on the Isle of Skye, drawing on the writer’s memories of childhood holidays at Talland House in St Ives, Cornwall. Woolf herself described it as “easily the best” of her books. Her sister, the artist Vanessa Bell, designed the original dust jacket.
firstSentence: “Yes, of course, if it’s fine tomorrow,” said Mrs Ramsay. “But you’ll have to be up with the lark.”

title: Ulysses
author: James Joyce
blurb: The modernist behemoth that mapped one day in Dublin – 16 June 1904 – and changed literature for ever. Originally conceived as a short story for his collection Dubliners, written over a seven-year period and banned in the US and the UK for obscenity before it was even published as a complete book, Joyce’s sprawling, stream-of-consciousness take on Homer’s Odyssey is one of the most challenging and rewarding novels written in English.
firstSentence: “Stately, plump Buck Mulligan came from the stairhead, bearing a bowl of lather on which a mirror and a razor lay crossed.”

title: Beloved
author: Toni Morrison
blurb: Winner of the Pulitzer prize for fiction, Morrison’s devastating account of formerly enslaved people after the American civil war was loosely based on the life of Margaret Garner, who killed her own daughter to spare her from being forced back into slavery. The novelist described Beloved as a story about “the pitched battle between remembering and forgetting”. This uncanny, literally haunted portrait of both physical and psychological violence remains one of the most banned and challenged books in American libraries, and one of the most cherished. In 1993, Morrison became the first Black woman to be awarded the Nobel prize in literature.
firstSentence: “124 was spiteful. Full of a baby’s venom.”

title: Middlemarch
author: George Eliot
blurb: Following the lives and loves of the inhabitants of a provincial English town in the middle of the 19th century, Eliot’s sixth novel is widely recognised as her masterpiece. Though she originally planned to write two separate books, Eliot merged them to create an intricately patterned epic that explores work and marriage, ambition and creativity, selfishness and community spirit against a background of political, social and technological change. An immediate bestseller, it has shaped literature in English ever since; few will be surprised to see it at the top of our list. As Emily Dickinson wrote: “What do I think of Middlemarch? What do I think of glory?”
firstSentence: “Miss Brooke had that kind of beauty which seems to be thrown into relief by poor dress.”
